original_title: House Of The Dragon burst its own bubble
summary_en: After years of buildup, the highly anticipated death of Ser Criston Cole in House of the Dragon's third season finale felt surprisingly underwhelming. The once-promising warrior's journey from Kingsguard to vengeful outcast culminated in a swift, unceremonious demise that left many viewers feeling deflated.

en.title: House of the Dragon: Criston Cole's Anticlimactic End Leaves Fans Wanting More
en.summary: After years of buildup, the highly anticipated death of Ser Criston Cole in House of the Dragon's third season finale felt surprisingly underwhelming. The once-promising warrior's journey from Kingsguard to vengeful outcast culminated in a swift, unceremonious demise that left many viewers feeling deflated.
en.body:
## The Warrior's Fall From Grace

For fans of **House of the Dragon**, the name **Criston Cole** has long been synonymous with a particular brand of self-inflicted misery and burning resentment. Ever since his bitter rejection by Princess Rhaenyra in season one, which led him to break his Kingsguard vows, Cole transformed into a fervent antagonist. His unwavering anti-Rhaenyra agenda, fueled by his perceived betrayal and a deep-seated sense of injustice, became a driving force for his actions, particularly his allegiance to **Alicent Hightower**. This simmering conflict set the stage for what many viewers expected to be a climactic confrontation or a meaningful end for the disgraced knight. Cole himself seemed to anticipate his demise, confessing his weariness and awaiting death. Even his allies, like **Gwayne Hightower**, seemed to grasp the perilous path he was treading, especially as his forces dwindled and crucial support from **Aemond** and **Vhagar** failed to materialize.

His isolation from **Alicent**, his self-proclaimed "beacon," further underscored his precarious position. The show spent considerable time charting Cole's march from King's Landing in season two towards Harrenhal, building anticipation for his ultimate fate. However, when his end finally arrived in "Faceless Men," it was far from the epic showdown many had envisioned. Instead, the mighty warrior, once a celebrated figure, was felled by a volley of arrows from **Alysanne Blackwood** within mere minutes of the episode's start. This abrupt and unceremonious end felt less like a dramatic conclusion to a complex character arc and more like the show quickly swatting away an annoying, albeit significant, fly.

## A Fan's Frustration

The anticipation for **Criston Cole's** downfall was palpable. His transformation from a loyal Kingsguard knight to a bitter, vengeful figure, particularly his obsessive hatred for Rhaenyra, made him a character many viewers loved to hate and eagerly awaited seeing meet his comeuppance. The extended setup, stretching across seasons, only amplified these expectations. Consequently, when his death arrived so swiftly and with such little fanfare, it left a significant portion of the fanbase feeling a sense of anticlimax. The narrative had invested so much in his personal vendetta and his internal struggles that his final moments felt like a missed opportunity for a more impactful resolution, leaving viewers questioning the show's storytelling priorities and the payoff for years of character development.

## What's Next

With **Criston Cole** now out of the picture, the focus of **House of the Dragon** will undoubtedly shift further towards the escalating conflict between the Greens and the Blacks. The remaining episodes of the season are expected to delve deeper into the consequences of recent events and the strategic moves that will shape the impending Dance of the Dragons. Details regarding the release schedule for the remainder of season three have not yet been announced, but anticipation is high for how the show will navigate the next crucial stages of the Targaryen civil war.

content_raw: This article discusses plot points from season three, episode six of House Of The Dragon, “ Faceless Men .”   Criston Cole’s annihilation is the moment every House Of The Dragon viewer has been waiting and loudly wishing for. Ever since he s rejection in season one —after he broke his Kingsguard vows, no less—Criston became a certified Westerosi incel. Devastated that a 16-year-old princess wouldn’t abandon her crown to run off to Essos with him, Criston swiftly switched his allegiance to Alicent Hightower in order to bring down his former lover. Criston’s anti-Rhaenyra agenda continued for decades—which leads us to season three, “Faceless Men,” and a highly anticipated death that now feels deflating in hindsight.  How did we get here? It didn’t help that the character was looking forward to meeting his maker: For a long time, Criston had been confessing that he awaits death. (No wonder Gwayne Hightower, despite his complicated feelings for the guy, jumped ship from the Riverlands and his commander’s suicide mission.) Criston predicted his end was near, considering his men and supplies dwindled and Aemond (Ewan Mitchell) was a no-show to assist him with Vhagar. He was also away from Alicent, his so-called “beacon,” who has enough problems to deal with to spare him a thought. HOTD has taken its time setting up Criston’s demise—practically ever since he left King’s Landing in season two to march toward Harrenhal. But when it finally happens, it’s nothing more than the show swatting an annoying fly out of the way as unceremoniously as possible.  Mere minutes into “ Faceless Men ,”  the realm’s self-proclaimed greatest warrior is felled by three arrows from the bow of Alysanne Blackwood. It should be a victory not just for Team Black, but also for the audience, who’ve patiently waited for years to see Ser Criston get his comeuppance. There’s no big swordfight, no honor, and no hero moment. Unfortunately for him, nobody is going to sing about his valor and misguided righteousness—certainly not in any way that will reach a wary Alicent’s ears. House Of The Dragon doesn’t give much weight to the depiction of Criston’s death—the Butcher’s Ball, as it’s called in George R.R. Martin’s Fire & Blood . Heck, Aemond stabbing a vulnerable Simon Strong (Simon Russell Beale) three episodes ago evoked a stronger reaction from me.  Criston’s anticlimactic exit mostly stays true to the source material. But it’s emblematic of a larger problem that has plagued House Of The Dragon from the start. In season one, the show frenetically (and often pleasantly) rushed through plot, introducing a young Rhaenyra as King Viserys’ chosen heir and ending with Emma D’Arcy’s older, jaded rendition of the princess grieving her dead dad and lost throne.
